description:
PROGRESS 2026-08-05.

DONE: ssnv101a (VMIS_CIN2_CHAB) verified against code_aster to 1.7e-5 relative on EPXX, EPXY and V1. Harness at crates/outram-park-fork-offbeat/tests/astest_ssnv101a.rs — reuse its pattern rather than reinventing: derive the stress from the .mail coordinates plus AFFE_CHAR_MECA forces (consistent nodal force = traction*area/4; a node with DDL_IMPO on a component contributes a reaction, not an applied force), CONFIRM the derivation by predicting the other free nodes and checking them against the deck, then drive stress-controlled with a fixed point on the elastic compliance.

ssnv113a (VISC_IRRA_LOG) IS UNUSABLE. Its .export declares 'F nom ssnv113a_mater.py D 0' and that file is absent from the clone; astest carries no *_mater.py at all. Measured across all 4,597 .export manifests: only 19 declare a missing input, so this is an exception, not a pattern — and ssnv113a is the only affected deck among our candidates. DO NOT go looking for the file: code_aster's 'data' repository is described upstream as material data that cannot be freely distributed, and DATA_POLICY.md puts it out of scope. Treat the deck as unusable.

REMAINING CANDIDATES, all with inputs present, all harder than ssnv101a in a specific way:
  ssnv101b  VMIS_CIN2_CHAB  2D, two QUAD4 elements, COEF(t)=50t, 30 steps. Same law already covered, so low marginal value.
  ssnv172b  VISC_CIN1_CHAB  C_PLAN (plane stress), 2D QUAD4, 4 elements. NEW law. Plane stress needs the out-of-plane condition solved.
  ssnv124b  NORTON_HOFF     3D_INCO_UPG (incompressible mixed u/p/g formulation), 16 elements. NEW law but the formulation is a real obstacle.
  ssnv126a  VENDOCHAB       3D single HEXA8, 32 reference values — the richest — but ANISOTHERMAL, 1000->1025 K, with three temperature-function material blocks (ELAS_FO, LEMAITRE_FO, VENDOCHAB_FO).

RECOMMENDED NEXT: ssnv126a. It is the only remaining single-element 3D case, it carries the most reference values by a wide margin, and the temperature-function material blocks are ordinary interpolation rather than a change of formulation — cheaper to handle than plane stress or an incompressible mixed element. It also exercises the damage module, where two upstream defects were deliberately reproduced, so it is the case most likely to be informative about them.

---

description:
Observed twice on 2026-08-11. The tests alpha_nightly::stable_transfer_functions::recurrence_tests::pid_step_cost_does_not_grow_with_step_index and its beta_testing sibling assert on measured wall-clock per-step cost. Both failed once and passed on immediate rerun while four other agents were compiling on the same machine.

WHY THIS MATTERS MORE THAN A USUAL FLAKE. These tests exist to defend the op-fm5 fix — they are the regression guard proving the response vectors no longer grow without bound. A guard that cries wolf gets muted, and the defect it guards against (a plateau at ~28 us/step at dt=0.04, degrading to ~1133 us/step at dt=0.001) is exactly the kind that creeps back in silently.

THE UNDERLYING ISSUE: wall-clock time is not the property under test. The property is that per-step cost is O(1) in the step index, i.e. that internal state does not grow. Wall-clock is a proxy for that, and a poor one on a shared machine.

SUGGESTED FIX: assert on the invariant directly rather than its timing shadow. Assert the internal state SIZE is constant between step 100 and step 100000 — a first-order recurrence keeps a fixed number of coefficients regardless of how many inputs it has seen. That is deterministic, machine-independent, fast, and it fails for the right reason. Note first_order_transfer_fn.rs already gained a state_size() method today (currently dead_code); that is the accessor this needs.

Keep a wall-clock benchmark if it is useful, but make it a benchmark that reports rather than a test that fails.

notes.author: teddy0@arch-aftershock-rapid-glass-S267454
notes.content:
SUBSTANTIALLY FIXED 2026-08-11 (agent stopped at session end mid-verification; needs a review pass).

The wall-clock flakiness was addressed by changing WHAT is asserted rather than loosening a threshold. The tests now measure a mean-cost window at step 5,000 and again at step 100,000 and assert the RATIO, with a deliberately loose 5x pass criterion. The ratio is machine-independent; the absolute microseconds are not. Measured on AMD Ryzen 5 5600, rustc 1.97.0, release: filtered PID with tau_d = 80.8 s gives 0.279 us/step at both windows, ratio 1.00; a bare P controller 0.105 -> 0.104 us/step, ratio 1.00. Stable across three consecutive runs (32/32 each, ratios 1.00-1.03).

The doc comment now states explicitly that those figures were taken under heavy concurrent build load, which is why they sit above the 0.17 us/step measured on an idle machine — recorded rather than hidden, so a future reader is not confused by the discrepancy. For contrast it also records the pre-0.2.0 behaviour on the same machine: 58.2 us/step at step 1,000 rising to 2329.5 us/step at step 79,000, a ratio of 40 and still climbing.

REMAINING: the agent was stopped with the message 'Let me update the recorded V&V numbers to match the new methodology and re-verify.' The alpha_nightly tier doc comment was verified complete during the session-end sweep; the beta_testing tier was NOT individually inspected. Both files were modified and 32/32 tests pass, so nothing is broken, but the beta tier's recorded numbers should be read against its actual methodology before this bead is closed.

Also still open as originally filed: asserting on internal STATE SIZE rather than timing at all would be strictly better — deterministic, machine-independent, and it fails for the right reason. first_order_transfer_fn.rs has a state_size() method (currently dead_code) which is the accessor for it.

description:
Maintainer asked 2026-08-05 about using the NASA GISS Panoply colorbars (https://www.giss.nasa.gov/tools/panoply/colorbars/) for temperature colouring, and flagged uncertainty about the copyright. That uncertainty was correct.

FINDING -- DO NOT ADOPT PANOPLY'S SET IN BULK (checked 2026-08-05):
The Panoply colorbars page carries NO licence, terms of use, or redistribution statement of any kind. The tables are explicitly third-party in origin, by the page's own attribution text:
  CB*   -> ColorBrewer2.org, Cynthia A. Brewer
  NCL*  -> NCL Graphics Color Table Gallery, UCAR
  GMT*  -> Generic Mapping Tools, SOEST, University of Hawai'i
  EO/NEO-> NASA Earth Observatory / NASA Earth Observations
  plus NOAA, UK Met Office, Scientific Visualization Studio, and individual researchers (e.g. Joshua Stevens)

So 'it is NASA, therefore public domain' does not hold: US Government works are public domain only for the parts NASA actually authored, and the page does not mark which those are. Taking the CB* tables via Panoply would additionally STRIP the attribution notice ColorBrewer's own licence requires. This fails RESEARCH_INTEGRITY_AND_PROVENANCE.md (documented source/author/licence/URL/date) and the CLAUDE.md rule against introducing code whose licence has not been checked.

TWO VERIFIED, GPL-3.0-COMPATIBLE ALTERNATIVES:

1. RECOMMENDED -- Scientific colour maps, Fabio Crameri.
   Licence: MIT (verified on the Zenodo record, v8.0.1, published 2023-10-05).
   DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.1243862 ; https://www.fabiocrameri.ch/colourmaps/
   Built for scientific data: perceptually uniform (equal steps in temperature look like equal steps in colour) and readable with colour-vision deficiency. Diverging hot/cold candidates: vik, roma. Sequential: lajolla, lipari. Citable, which suits the V&V write-ups.

2. ColorBrewer. Licence: Apache-2.0, (c) 2002 Cynthia Brewer, Mark Harrower, The Pennsylvania State University.
   GPL-3.0-compatible (NOT GPL-2-compatible). Conditions: retain the copyright notice; end-user documentation must acknowledge 'This product includes color specifications and designs developed by Cynthia Brewer (http://colorbrewer.org/)'; the ColorBrewer name may not be used to endorse derivatives.

HOW TO IMPLEMENT WHEN PICKED UP:
  - ADD alongside the existing maps, never replace them. crates/outram-park-digital-twin-engine/src/color_maps/ is documented as already-validated code whose exact values call sites depend on. hot_to_cold_colour_mark_1 stays.
  - New map gets a provenance header (project, author, version/DOI, licence, URL, date accessed) and a References.md entry.
  - If ColorBrewer is chosen, the attribution string above must appear in user-facing docs, not just source.

Callers that would benefit: PipeVisual cell fills, TurbineVisual casing, and the per-stage steam-quality tint (which currently reuses steam_quality_colour_mark_1 normalised over a display range).

notes.author: teddy0@snrsi-arch-desktop
notes.content:
COLORBREWER SOURCE CLARIFICATION (checked 2026-08-06, prompted by the maintainer asking whether github.com/axismaps/colorbrewer is 'the' ColorBrewer):

Yes -- axismaps/colorbrewer is the official repository behind colorbrewer2.org, maintained by Axis Maps, with the schemes based on Dr Cynthia Brewer's research.

BUT THE TWO LICENCE FILES ARE NOT INTERCHANGEABLE:
  - github.com/axismaps/colorbrewer/LICENCE.txt is the STOCK Apache-2.0 boilerplate with the placeholders left unfilled ('Copyright {yyyy} {name of copyright owner}'). It names no copyright holder and carries no acknowledgement clause. It governs Axis Maps' website/software.
  - colorbrewer2.org/export/LICENSE.txt is Apache-2.0 WITH the copyright filled in -- (c) 2002 Cynthia Brewer, Mark Harrower, The Pennsylvania State University -- and the specific condition that end-user documentation acknowledge: 'This product includes color specifications and designs developed by Cynthia Brewer (http://colorbrewer.org/)'. It also forbids using the ColorBrewer name to endorse derivatives.

The colour SPECIFICATIONS are the part this project would use, so the export licence is the authoritative one to cite. Taking the GitHub boilerplate instead would mean redistributing the colour data with no named copyright holder and no attribution -- the same defect as taking them via Panoply.

Unchanged recommendation: Crameri's Scientific colour maps (MIT, DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1243862) remain the simpler choice, with no attribution clause to carry and better suitability for scientific data. ColorBrewer stays viable if its acknowledgement is honoured in user-facing docs.

notes.author: teddy0@snrsi-arch-desktop
notes.content:
DECIDED 2026-08-06 (maintainer): use CRAMERI'S SCIENTIFIC COLOUR MAPS. ColorBrewer is not being adopted; the licence comparison above is retained only as the record of why.

Licence: MIT. Verified on the Zenodo record, v8.0.1, published 2023-10-05.
Cite: Crameri, F. (2018). Scientific colour maps. Zenodo. DOI 10.5281/zenodo.1243862
Home: https://www.fabiocrameri.ch/colourmaps/  Supporting paper: Geoscientific Model Development (2018).
MIT is compatible with this workspace's GPL-3.0-only and carries no attribution clause to thread through user-facing docs.

WHY CRAMERI RATHER THAN COLORBREWER (the reason is technical, not preference):
ColorBrewer's schemes were designed to make DISCRETE choropleth classes distinguishable and are NOT perceptually uniform. Stretched across a continuous field they manufacture apparent banding -- fast-changing stretches read as steep gradients and flat stretches as isothermal, when the underlying data is smooth. For widgets whose stated premise is that rendering derives directly from physics state, a colour map that invents structure is actively wrong. Crameri's are perceptually uniform by construction: equal steps in the quantity read as equal steps in colour.

Two further properties that matter here:
  - Greyscale-safe: stays readable printed black-and-white, which the V&V write-ups will need.
  - CYCLIC maps (romaO, vikO, ...). ColorBrewer has no equivalent, and the turbine rotor angle is a cyclic quantity -- a cyclic map is the correct way to colour one.

ColorBrewer's qualitative sets remain the more battle-tested option IF categorical palettes are ever wanted (flow regimes, component types, material IDs). Revisit only for that.

MAP SELECTION (suggested, confirm when implementing):
  - temperature / hot-cold, diverging: vik or roma
  - sequential (quality, burnup, flux): lajolla, lipari, or batlow
  - cyclic (rotor angle, phase): romaO or vikO

IMPLEMENTATION CONSTRAINTS (unchanged):
  - ADD alongside the existing maps; never replace them. crates/outram-park-digital-twin-engine/src/color_maps/ is documented as already-validated code whose exact values call sites depend on. hot_to_cold_colour_mark_1 and steam_quality_colour_mark_1 both stay.
  - Provenance header on the new module (project, author, version, DOI, licence, URL, date accessed) plus a References.md entry, per RESEARCH_INTEGRITY_AND_PROVENANCE.md.
  - Vendor only the specific map tables used, with their MIT notice, rather than the whole suite.
  - Callers that would benefit: PipeVisual cell fills, TurbineVisual casing, the per-stage steam-quality tint.

notes.author: teddy0@snrsi-arch-desktop
notes.content:
NEUTRAL-MIDPOINT ALTERNATIVES (measured 2026-08-06, from the official archive). Maintainer asked whether anything other than white could carry 'neither hot nor cold'; decision was to KEEP WHITE (vik). Recorded so the option is not re-derived.

Diverging maps in the suite, sampled at t=0 / t=0.5 / t=1 with Rec.601 luma at the midpoint:
  vik      (  0, 18, 97) (236,229,224) ( 89,  0,  8)  mid-luma 230.5   <- in use
  broc     ( 44, 26, 76) (235,238,236) ( 38, 38,  0)  236.9
  cork     ( 44, 25, 76) (230,237,236) ( 15, 41,  3)  234.8
  bam      (101,  2, 75) (246,241,240) ( 13, 76,  0)  242.4
  roma     (126, 23,  0) (192,234,195) (  3, 49,152)  217.0
  berlin   (158,176,255) ( 25, 12,  9) (255,173,173)   15.5   <- dark neutral
  lisbon   (230,229,255) ( 23, 25, 25) (255,255,217)   24.4
  tofino   (222,217,255) ( 13, 22, 19) (219,230,155)   19.0
  vanimo   (255,205,253) ( 26, 21, 19) (190,253,165)   22.3
  managua  (255,207,103) ( 87, 41, 73) (129,231,255)   58.4

berlin is the direct drop-in if a dark neutral is ever wanted: same blue-cold / red-hot semantics, but the midpoint recedes on a dark UI instead of being the brightest thing on screen.

WHY WHITE WAS KEPT: berlin and the other dark-neutral maps invert the intensity relationship -- extremes become light, the middle dark -- so they read oddly printed or on a light background. vik behaves sensibly either way, which matters if studio output ends up in figures. Switching is a one-line change in components::temperature_colour; the blue/white/red convention test would need updating with it.
